dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — Benji is six days old, and it's a cold, damp Saturday made for staying in with him. Overnight, Qatar says its mediation between the U.S. and Iran is still alive, while Russia hit Kyiv with a massive missile and drone barrage ahead of next week's peace talks in Abu Dhabi. At home, Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff on Monday, the first big shake-up after the midterm rout. Solon starts wet with morning showers and a high near 47°, clearing later, so errands are better this afternoon. Sports is stacked from the couch: Ohio State football hosts Oregon at 3:30 PM in a playoff survival game, the Cavs host the Knicks at 8 PM after routing the 76ers 119-95 last night, and locally the Ohio Hazmat Teams Conference wraps up today at the Solon Community Center.

Solon's week starts cold and damp Saturday at 47°, breaks milder Sunday through Tuesday with a mostly sunny 60° peak, then turns sharply colder late in the week with rain changing to rain and snow by Friday. The sports weekend is loaded: Ohio State hosts Oregon Saturday afternoon, the Cavs play the Knicks Saturday night after Friday's 119-95 rout of Philadelphia, and the Browns visit the Saints Sunday with Shedeur Sanders starting. The standout grocery move is still the Thanksgiving stock-up — Meijer brand frozen turkeys at 79¢/lb or less through November 26 beat Giant Eagle's 95¢/lb — and close to home, the Hazmat Teams Conference wraps up in Solon today while Día de Muertos celebrates in Cleveland.

Qatar says U.S.-Iran mediation is still alive, denies reports talks failed
items.summary:
Qatar pushed back on Saturday against online claims that its effort to broker an understanding between Washington and Tehran had collapsed. In a statement from its International Media Office, Doha said remarks by Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani had been distorted, and that both sides were still working toward an agreement with Qatari officials in close contact with each capital.

The prime minister, speaking to Al Jazeera, said the mediation was meant to keep the regional confrontation from spinning further out of control and that meaningful progress had already been made. He argued the goal should be a workable settlement rather than waiting for a perfect one, and said Washington's interest in finding a solution had not shifted after Tuesday's midterm elections.

That diplomatic line is running in parallel with renewed military tension. Iranian semi-official reporting on Saturday mentioned two missile impacts on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, with no confirmed damage assessment, while the United States had not at that point formally announced a new attack inside Iran.

What to watch is whether Qatar can turn the current exchange of proposals into a concrete interim step. Tehran has been floating a multi-day plan since September that links reopening Hormuz to lifting a port blockade and unfreezing assets — an approach Washington has so far rejected — so the gap on sequencing remains the central obstacle.

items.title: Iran is reviewing Qatari proposals on its nuclear program, but sets conditions first
items.summary:
Iran is studying proposals passed through Qatar that would bring its nuclear activities into a negotiation with the United States, according to two regional government officials who spoke Friday. The fact Tehran is even reviewing language on a file it had previously kept off the table marks a small opening after more than eight months of war.

The opening comes with a hard condition. Iranian officials say they will not negotiate the nuclear question until Washington meets a set of demands tied to a ceasefire, including sanctions relief, release of frozen funds, an end to the blockade of Iranian ports, and compensation. U.S. officials, by contrast, insist nuclear limits have to be part of any early discussion, and the White House declined to comment on the Qatari package while President Donald Trump told reporters Friday that contacts with Iran were continuing.

Mediators have discussed a short bridge arrangement to build trust over about two days — first steps such as easing the blockade and releasing some frozen money, followed by Iran reopening the Strait of Hormuz under a modified arrangement previously discussed with Oman but not approved by Washington. Qatar's emir spoke with Trump on Friday about de-escalation, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke with his Qatari counterpart, and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi worked regional capitals by phone.

Why it matters is timing. The review follows days after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in the midterms, a result widely linked in exit polling and internal Republican debate to the unpopularity of the Iran war, which raises pressure on the White House to show a diplomatic path even as limited strikes continue.

items.title: Russia hits Kyiv with a massive overnight missile and drone barrage ahead of peace talks
items.summary:
Missile explosions shook Kyiv overnight into Saturday, wounding at least nine people, just days before Ukrainian, Russian and American negotiators are due to meet in Abu Dhabi. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones at the capital and surrounding region, damaging homes, commercial buildings and critical infrastructure.

City and national authorities said the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River was hit and closed to traffic, a kindergarten and residential buildings were damaged, and new power and water outages followed strikes on energy facilities. Ukraine's air force said defenses intercepted many of the incoming drones and several missiles, but impacts were reported across Kyiv and more than a dozen other regions, with substations linked to nuclear power plants among the targets Zelensky cited.

Russia's Defense Ministry confirmed it targeted the bridge, saying it was used to move weapons and military equipment, and said it also struck an industrial site in Kyiv linked to missile production, a power station and an ammunition plant in the wider region. Moscow also claimed it shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian regions, a figure that was not independently verified, while Ukraine said its own strikes hit a refinery in Saratov and an electronics plant in Oryol.

The barrage matters because it lands on the eve of the first trilateral talks since February, scheduled for November 10-11. Zelensky framed the attack as Russia negotiating with missiles, and the damage to Kyiv's power supply — described by Mayor Vitali Klitschko as extremely difficult — will shape what Ukraine asks for on energy ceasefires and air defense at the table.
items.source: Gazette Herald / PA via Ukrinform reporting

items.title: Russia names senior team for Abu Dhabi trilateral talks with the U.S. and Ukraine
items.summary:
The Kremlin confirmed on Saturday who Russia will send to next week's trilateral meeting with the United States and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Interfax the delegation will be led in part by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, joined by Deputy Foreign Ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin.

The team will also include Igor Kostyukov, head of Russia's military intelligence service, and Yuri Zhigarlovsky, a senior officer from the General Staff, alongside other diplomatic and military officials. The inclusion of both senior diplomats and top military intelligence and General Staff figures signals Moscow is preparing to discuss security guarantees and battlefield arrangements, not only political language.

On the other sides of the table, Ukraine's delegation is expected to be led by presidential office head Kyrylo Budanov, while the U.S. mediating team is expected to be led by special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The White House has also outlined a broader European security framework discussed in Brussels this week with Ukrainian, NATO and European partners, covering crisis communications, military transparency and long-term stability arrangements, though European representatives will not sit in the Abu Dhabi trilateral itself.

What to watch is whether the November 10-11 session produces anything beyond a humanitarian step, such as prisoner exchanges or a pause on energy strikes. The core disputes — ceasefire lines, territory, security guarantees and Ukraine's future alignment — remain unresolved, and this week's strikes underline how far apart the parties still are.

items.title: Paraguay's Senate removes President Peña, who is placed under house arrest in bank collapse
items.summary:
Paraguay's Senate removed President Santiago Peña from office on Friday in a 44-0 vote among senators present, and within an hour authorities placed him under house arrest. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in soon afterward and will serve the remainder of the term, which runs to August 2028.

The crisis centers on ueno, a digital bank that regulators seized on November 3 after its solvency fell below half the required level. The collapse froze access for nearly three million customers — close to half the country's population — and prosecutors opened multiple criminal cases, citing suspected breach of trust and saying charges could extend to influence peddling. Former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo, installed by Peña, was also covered by the arrest order.

Peña had tried to resign on Thursday, but Congress refused the resignation and pressed ahead with impeachment, which also strips his parliamentary immunity. The lower house had already voted 78-0 to impeach. He was ordered to report to prosecutors on Saturday morning and denies the process should be treated as proof of criminal guilt, while his lawyers challenged the legal basis of the proceedings.

Why it matters goes beyond one presidency. A banking failure that touched so many households in days has become a test of Paraguay's institutions — whether depositors get access restored quickly under Alliana, and whether the investigation stays focused on the bank's finances and any conflicts of interest around it.

items.title: Third wave of hoax bomb threats disrupts at least 18 more flights across Europe
items.summary:
A fresh wave of hoax bomb threats disrupted at least 18 flights across Europe on Friday, the third wave in a week, with every affected aircraft landing safely and searches finding no explosive devices. The alerts hit flights to or from Bulgaria, Cyprus, Czechia, France, Hungary, Italy, Portugal, Romania and the United Kingdom, and also targeted media organizations in Ireland and Britain.

Earlier in the week at least 35 flights had already been diverted or searched. Fighter jets were scrambled in several countries to escort civilian planes, a Wizz Air flight from Prague to Rome diverted to Venice, a Ryanair flight from London to Sofia landed in Plovdiv, and Prague reported at least nine affected flights on Friday morning alone. Eurocontrol noted the disrupted services were a tiny fraction of the 26,709 flights scheduled in Europe that day, but each specific threat triggers mandatory landing, evacuation and specialist searches.

Some messages on Thursday were signed in the name of the Male State, a Russian far-right ultranationalist movement founded in 2016, which has denied involvement and said it ceased to exist in 2021. Investigators said Friday they had not established evidence linking the campaign to a hostile state or terrorist group, including Russia or Iran, though European officials have described the pattern as an apparently coordinated effort to cause chaos and psychological pressure.

What to watch is attribution and copycats. Authorities across cyber, aviation and defense agencies are tracing the emails, and officials warn that even a known hoax pattern cannot be ignored when a threat names a flight already in the air.
items.source: The Guardian via World Right Now

items.title: Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff
items.summary:
Susie Wiles is leaving as White House chief of staff days after Republicans lost their House and Senate majorities, and President Donald Trump announced Friday she will be replaced by longtime aide Stephen Miller effective Monday, November 9. Wiles, the first woman to hold the job and Trump's 2024 campaign manager, will move to his political operation.

People familiar with the matter told CNN Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday evening as Trump grew furious watching coverage of the historic midterm losses and blamed his political strategy team. Trump publicly praised Wiles as having done an outstanding job and said the change was not because of the election, calling it simply time to make a move, while also praising Miller as someone who has been with him from the beginning and is very good politically.

Miller, 41, has been deputy chief of staff and the architect of the administration's hardline immigration agenda, widening his influence across domestic policy and pushing an expansive view of executive power. His elevation, after he directed daily pressure on Homeland Security officials and previously pushed for very high daily immigration arrest targets that the White House has denied were quotas, signals the administration intends to double down rather than pivot after the defeat, a reading shared by officials who spoke to CNN and by Democratic critics who immediately said he should prepare for congressional scrutiny.

The human and political stakes inside the building are immediate. Wiles, who recently completed treatment after a breast cancer diagnosis in March, had been seen by aides as the person who kept operations running, and some officials called her departure a catastrophic loss. What to watch is who else leaves, how Miller reorganizes the West Wing, and how the incoming Democratic Congress — especially the House Oversight Committee — targets his role.

items.title: Trump signals more Cabinet changes after Wiles exit in '60 Minutes' interview
items.summary:
President Donald Trump signaled in a '60 Minutes' interview taped Friday morning that the departure of chief of staff Susie Wiles will not be the only personnel change after the Republican midterm defeat. Asked whether he expected to fire anyone, he said he did, a little bit, while insisting he loves his Cabinet.

The preview, released Friday night ahead of Sunday's full broadcast at 7 p.m. ET, was recorded just hours before Trump announced on Truth Social that Stephen Miller would take over as chief of staff on Monday and Wiles would move to the Trump Political Operation. Correspondent Ross Douthat pressed him on confidence in his team, including War Secretary Pete Hegseth, whose leadership of the Iran war has drawn Republican criticism after the losses.

Trump declined to name who else might go, saying he did not want to mention names. The administration has already seen several senior departures this year, and speculation in Washington has focused on officials tied to the Iran war and to immigration enforcement, though no additional dismissals had been confirmed as of Saturday morning.

Why it matters is control of the narrative for the next two years. With Democrats set to take both chambers in January, personnel moves are Trump's most direct way to show a response to voters without changing policy, and the Sunday interview will be parsed for whether he frames further changes as accountability or as a tightening of loyalist control.

items.title: Democrats sweep both chambers, putting Hakeem Jeffries in line to be first Black Speaker
items.summary:
Democrats seized control of both the House and the Senate in Tuesday's midterms, in one of the most consequential midterm reversals in modern history just two years after Republicans swept in 2024. NBC projected Democrats could finish with as many as 258 House seats to 177 for Republicans, and the party flipped seven Senate seats to reach at least 54, with a chance to grow to 56 depending on Alaska and Mississippi.

The Senate pickups came in Maine, Ohio, Kansas, Iowa, Texas, North Carolina and South Carolina — states Republicans had counted as part of a durable majority. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is now positioned to become the first Black Speaker in American history when the new Congress convenes January 3, and Senate leader Chuck Schumer celebrated what he called a historic victory rooted in voter rejection of high prices, the Iran war and the administration's agenda.

Two Senate races remained too close to call in the latest counts. In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola led Republican Dan Sullivan by only a few hundred votes with ranked-choice tabulation set for November 18, and in Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom led Cindy Hyde-Smith by a similarly tiny margin with most ballots counted, so the final size of the majority is still moving.

Governing will be harder than winning. Democrats will control committees, subpoena power and the legislative agenda for Trump's final two years, but they still face a presidential veto and the Senate's 60-vote threshold for most bills. What to watch is the November 18-19 House Democratic leadership elections and whether the large House margin gives Jeffries room to set an affordability-focused agenda he campaigned on.

items.title: Petition against Jeffries for Speaker tops 920,000 as Democrats argue over leadership
items.summary:
Even as Hakeem Jeffries' path to the speakership remains clear inside the House, Democratic offices have been flooded since Tuesday with calls and emails urging lawmakers to deny him the gavel. More than a dozen lawmakers and aides told Axios the pressure has poured in since Democrats retook the House, driven in large part by a Change.org petition that listed more than 921,000 verified signatures by Friday afternoon.

The petition argues the speaker should better represent Democratic voters and urges every member of the incoming 120th Congress to vote against Jeffries in January. Progressive organizers, including Indivisible co-executive director Ezra Levin, have amplified the campaign, while parallel discontent in the Senate has seen some newly elected senators questioning whether Chuck Schumer should continue as Democratic leader after the sweep.

Inside the Capitol, the math still favors Jeffries. NBC projects at least 258 Democratic House seats, a level the party has not reached since 1993, and Jeffries would need only a majority of votes cast for named candidates on the floor on January 3. House Democrats hold their internal leadership elections November 18-19, which will show whether the outside petition translates into an actual challenger or a protest vote.

Why it matters is mandate versus unity. Democrats won on a disciplined affordability message, and a public leadership fight in the first weeks could complicate their attempt to present a governing alternative to Trump, even if Jeffries ultimately wins comfortably.

items.title: Vance blames the Iran war for the midterm loss and privately blasts Netanyahu
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance publicly blamed the Iran war for Republicans losing Congress, writing on X that the reason the party lost is the war and adding that the president himself had said so the night before. Axios reported November 4-5 that Vance had also privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being wrong on everything regarding Iran.

According to the reporting, Vance warned colleagues the war was deeply unpopular and could cost Republicans the election, and he has led a faction of senior officials urging Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement rather than resume major strikes. Netanyahu, by contrast, had urged Trump to resume strikes ahead of the midterms, while Trump held off after endorsing Netanyahu for reelection in Israel. Vance last month also sent a letter through Qatari intermediaries to a top Iranian security official proposing renewed negotiations, with any talks to address Iran's nuclear program.

Analysts quoted by Fox News noted the political dimension for 2028. Distancing himself from both the war and Netanyahu could benefit Vance if he runs for president, while Trump told The Wall Street Journal Iran was a piece of the defeat but said he did the right thing and would do it again, highlighting a gap between the president and his vice president.

What to watch is whether Vance's push for a deal gains ground now that Miller — a hawkish loyalist — controls the chief of staff's office, and whether the White House chooses negotiation, continued limited strikes, or a larger military campaign in the coming weeks.

items.title: Trump warns Democrats that impeaching him again would destroy them
items.summary:
President Donald Trump warned the newly victorious Democrats against impeaching him for a third time, saying such a move would destroy them politically after their historic midterm success gave them full control of Congress. The warning sets up the central confrontation of the next Congress before it has even been sworn in.

Democrats will take office in January with subpoena power, committee chairs and the ability to launch investigations into the administration, including into Stephen Miller, the Iran war and immigration enforcement. Trump, meanwhile, retains the veto, command of the executive branch and, with Miller's appointment on Friday, a chief of staff closely associated with the policies voters rejected on Tuesday.

Vance's post-election argument — that the war caused the defeat — was cited in the same coverage as evidence of internal Republican division, with the vice president privately arguing against the U.S.-led war while Trump defended his decisions. That split, plus Trump's promise of further Cabinet changes in his '60 Minutes' interview, suggests Republicans will spend the transition arguing over blame rather than presenting a unified response to the new majority.

Why it matters is restraint. Democrats campaigned on affordability, ending the Iran war and accountability, but a third impeachment would consume the new Congress and could, as Trump bets, shift public sympathy. What to watch is the first investigative targets House committees announce after the November 18-19 leadership elections, and whether Democratic leaders steer toward oversight hearings or straight to impeachment talk.

items.title: Wall Street ends the week mixed as tech bounces back
items.summary:
Friday's close split the market in two. The Nasdaq Composite rose 264.43 points, or 1.09%, to 24,579.42, and the S&P 500 added 0.31% to 7,376.86, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 237.33 points, or 0.46%, to 51,285.73. Buyers stepped back into technology names a day after a steep sell-off, but the rebound was not broad enough to lift the older industrial average.

The bounce did not erase the week. The S&P 500 still finished down 2.7% for the week, the Nasdaq down 3.4% and the Dow down 0.9% — the worst week for stocks since June in some recaps, and the S&P's biggest weekly drop since April 2025 in the Wall Street Journal's account. Thursday's rout, when the Nasdaq fell more than 5% and chip stocks collapsed, set the scale of what Friday could only partly repair.

Why it matters is the tension underneath the green tech close. A much stronger-than-expected October jobs report lifted Treasury yields — the 10-year reached about 4.86% — and raised expectations for another Federal Reserve rate increase in December. That caps how far a bargain-hunting rally can run if borrowing costs are headed higher again.

What to watch next is the October inflation report due November 10, the last major price reading before the Fed meets December 8-9. If inflation stays hot alongside strong hiring, the rate-hike case markets priced on Friday will harden.

items.title: Chip stocks rebound 4% after a 12% rout, led by AMD
items.summary:
Semiconductor shares led Friday's recovery after leading Thursday's collapse. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index rose 4.21% after tumbling more than 12% the day before, and the iShares Semiconductor ETF rose about 3.5%. Advanced Micro Devices jumped about 11%, Intel added roughly 8%, Micron rose about 5%, and Nvidia climbed nearly 3%, with TSMC and ASML also sharply higher in the broader tally.

The swing traces back to politics as much as earnings. Thursday's sell-off was driven by fears that the new Democratic majorities in Congress, and new Democratic governors in key states, would slow or restrict the data-center build-out that has powered demand for AI chips. Friday's buying suggests investors decided at least part of that fear was overdone for now, or simply that prices had fallen far enough to attract buyers.

The rebound still left the group well below where it started the week. Recovering roughly a third of a 12% drop is a bounce, not a full recovery, and related names told the same story — SanDisk gained about 3.5% after dropping 22% on Thursday, while data-center and cloud names such as CoreWeave and Nebius also rose.

What to watch is whether the policy risk becomes real legislation or local permitting fights. Proposals around data-center power costs, water use and tax breaks are now a live debate after the midterms, and chip demand depends heavily on how fast new capacity can actually be built.

items.title: Hiring beats forecasts by a wide margin in October
items.summary:
Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday, far above the roughly 59,000 to 65,000 economists had expected. The unemployment rate slipped to 4.1% from 4.2%, and September's gain was revised up to 60,000 from an initial 29,000, with August also revised higher — adding a combined 84,000 jobs to the earlier months.

Pay rose as well. Average hourly earnings increased 0.4% in the month, or 14 cents, to $38.00, for a 3.1% increase from a year earlier. Growth was strongest in professional and business services, health care, and transportation and warehousing in the detailed breakdowns reported Friday.

The stakes are mainly for the Federal Reserve. A labor market this firm, with wages still rising, gives officials less room to ease policy and more reason to worry that inflation will stay above their 2% target. Futures markets moved quickly, lifting the odds of a December rate hike to roughly 77%, up about 10 points from the day before.

One complication sits inside the headline strength. The number of people working part time for economic reasons rose by about 339,000 to roughly 4.8 million, a sign that not every worker who wants full-time hours is getting them. The November jobs report on December 4 and the October inflation data will test whether October was a genuine re-acceleration or a one-month surprise.

items.title: A top Fed official says more tightening is likely
items.summary:
San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said Friday that the central bank will likely need to raise interest rates further to bring inflation that remains too high back down. She made the case on CNBC even while acknowledging the sharp repricing in technology stocks this week.

Daly described the tech move as painful but orderly, as investors reassess how strong demand tied to artificial intelligence will actually be. That framing matters: a Fed official calling a sell-off orderly is signaling that market turbulence alone is not a reason to stop tightening.

Her prescription was for a deliberate, gradual path rather than a rushed one, precisely because conditions are volatile and the destination for rates is not yet clear. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack made a similar argument this week, saying policy would need to become restrictive to reach the inflation target, and both officials had supported a hike at the last meeting, when the Fed held its range at 3.75% to 4%.

What to watch is the December 8-9 meeting. With futures pricing a hike to 4% to 4.25% as the most likely outcome after the jobs report, the next inflation reading will be the deciding input — and officials like Daly are preparing markets for the idea that holding steady is not the default.

items.title: Anthropic's big IPO runs into a valuation fight
items.summary:
Anthropic's planned public offering, expected to be one of the largest technology listings ever, is facing pushback on price just as its roadshow was set to begin the week of November 9. The company had been discussed at around a $1.5 trillion valuation with a raise of up to $100 billion, but the Wall Street Journal reported that at least three major prospective investors believe that level will not hold, with one putting fair value closer to $1 trillion.

The financials explain both the excitement and the caution. Anthropic's amended filing showed third-quarter revenue of about $17 billion and a run rate above $80 billion by the end of October. Against that, the filing disclosed roughly $895 billion in long-term commitments for computing power, chips and infrastructure — spending that must be paid for whether demand matches the most optimistic forecasts or not.

Timing is making the argument harder. The company is trying to price into a market that just erased about $2.5 trillion from the Nasdaq on Thursday, amid a broader backlash against data-center expansion after the midterms. Analysts have already trimmed forecasts for new data-center capacity in 2030, which is exactly the resource Anthropic needs to train and run its Claude models.

Executives and advisers are expected to decide within days whether to accept a lower valuation, raise less — reports suggest $80 billion rather than $100 billion — or delay. A successful listing at a reset price could still be a landmark event; a weak debut, several strategists warned, would reverberate across the whole AI trade.

items.title: Airbnb and Cloudflare soar on earnings while DraftKings plunges
items.summary:
Earnings split the market sharply on Friday. Airbnb jumped about 12% after reporting third-quarter earnings of $3.16 a share against expectations of $2.85, on revenue of $4.87 billion, up 19% from a year earlier and above its own guidance. The company raised its full-year outlook to high-teens revenue growth and authorized a new $12 billion share buyback.

Cloudflare was the other standout, rising about 10% after beating third-quarter expectations and guiding fourth-quarter earnings to about 43 cents a share, ahead of Wall Street's view. Its revenue of about $782.5 million reinforced its place among the AI-adjacent infrastructure names investors still want to own after Thursday's washout.

The losers were just as dramatic. DraftKings fell about 21% after posting a wider-than-expected loss and revenue that missed forecasts, with its sportsbook business short of estimates. Five9, Axon and Atlassian also sold off hard after their results, showing how unforgiving this earnings season has been for any miss.

Why it matters is what the split says about the consumer and about expectations. Travel demand, at least as Airbnb measures it — nights and seats booked up 16%, app bookings up sharply, and first-time bookers accelerating — is still growing fast. But companies that miss, even modestly, are being punished as if growth is fragile everywhere else.

items.title: Newsom moves to commute every California death sentence
items.summary:
Governor Gavin Newsom announced November 5 that he is commuting all of California's death sentences to life in prison without parole, affecting 548 people — the largest mass commutation of death sentences in U.S. history. In an open letter he argued that state executions are unjust, prone to error and incompatible with California's values. No one covered by the plan will be released.

The legal path is only partly in his hands. Newsom can act directly for 166 people, but 382 others have more than one felony conviction, and California's Constitution requires the state Supreme Court to recommend clemency in those cases, with at least four of seven justices agreeing. He has asked the court, which currently has a vacancy, to act before the end of the year so he can finish the process before leaving office on January 4, 2027.

Reaction split sharply and quickly in the follow-up reporting November 6. Anti-death-penalty groups and some victims' relatives praised the move, while the California District Attorneys Association, several county prosecutors and other victims' families condemned it as disregarding juries, judges and voters — California voters rejected abolition in 2016 and instead approved a measure to speed executions. Riverside County's district attorney and sheriff said they were not consulted in advance, and noted 87 of the cases come from that county alone.

The contrast on the day of the announcement underlined the national divide: executions were carried out the same day in Florida, Indiana and Alabama. If the court approves the remaining cases, California's action alone would cut the national death-row population by nearly 30%, to its lowest level since 1984.

items.title: U.S. carries out new limited strikes on Iran near Hormuz
items.summary:
President Trump confirmed Friday evening, after arriving in West Palm Beach, Florida, that U.S. forces had carried out what he called minor strikes against an Iranian air-defense system on November 6. He said Iran had built a small anti-aircraft installation and that U.S. forces knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five. He did not provide operational details, and his account of the damage could not be independently verified.

Iranian media reported two explosions in the Suza area of Qeshm Island, at the entrance to the Persian Gulf near the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian outlets also claimed air defenses had downed American drones over the island. The United States has not confirmed any drone loss, and a Central Command official described the situation around Qeshm as relatively calm.

This was the second round of strikes on the same island in a week, following a November 2 operation U.S. officials described as defensive, and the first strikes reported since the November 3 midterms. Late Friday, the U.S. also publicized a Rewards for Justice offer of up to $20 million, plus possible relocation, for information about Iran's nuclear program, including its facilities, equipment and personnel.

Why it matters is the location and the diplomacy running alongside it. Qeshm sits beside the waterway that carries a large share of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas, so even limited strikes there move energy markets and raise escalation risk. At the same time, Trump said talks with Tehran are making progress and that Iran wants a deal, and Qatari mediators said they are still working to prevent a wider return to war — a combination that leaves the next move genuinely uncertain.

items.title: Two Senate races are still too close to call
items.summary:
Four days after the midterms, the Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska remain uncalled, even though control of the chamber is already settled. Democrats have won 54 seats to Republicans' 44, and these two races will decide only whether that majority grows.

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom held a lead of roughly 2,000 votes over Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith on Friday, about 49.1% to 48.8%, with more than 95% of ballots counted. Thousands of affidavit and provisional ballots still have to be reviewed, and mail ballots postmarked by Election Day can arrive until November 10. Mississippi has no automatic recount law, so any challenge would likely end up in court, and counties must certify by November 13.

In Alaska, former Democratic Representative Mary Peltola led Republican Senator Dan Sullivan by only about 600 votes, with roughly three-quarters of ballots counted. Alaska's ranked-choice system adds another layer: if no candidate clears 50% of first-choice votes, a tabulation of second choices is scheduled for November 18, and late mail and early ballots will not all be counted until November 10.

Both parties are already fundraising for the legal fight, with the Republican and Democratic Senate campaign arms creating recount funds and the Republican committee demanding that Mississippi officials preserve all affidavit ballots. The practical takeaway for the new Congress is timing — the final margin may not be certified in Mississippi until December 3, and Alaska's result could hinge on preferences that have not yet been published at all.

items.title: Voters reject data centers in town after town
items.summary:
Data centers were on the ballot in about 41 local measures on Election Day, and voters rejected development in 40 of them, according to Fortune's account citing Axios and Ballotpedia, with CNBC reporting the same tally. All six similar measures decided earlier in 2026 had also gone against development. The pattern held across states and party lines.

The objections driving the votes were mostly local and practical rather than abstract arguments about artificial intelligence: higher electricity bills, water use, noise, land use and tax breaks for very large companies. In several places the measures did not ban facilities outright but imposed limits — public votes for large projects, financial guarantees from developers seeking tax breaks, or noise and size caps. Sunbury, Ohio, for example, voted 79% to 21% to ban data centers over 25 megawatts after a proposed $2 billion Amazon campus.

State action followed the same direction. Texas paused new approvals pending an audit, and Senator Bernie Sanders called on Thursday for a national moratorium, while some Democratic lawmakers discussed far broader AI restrictions. Analysts split on the consequences: Goldman Sachs called a national moratorium unlikely, in part because the president could veto it, while UBS estimated roughly 30% of expected 2028 U.S. data-center capacity additions could be at risk.

The industry response started within two days. OpenAI published a National Community Compact on Thursday pledging to pay for the electricity and grid infrastructure for campuses it owns and operates, and to post financial guarantees before major spending so local customers are not left with the bill if a project is delayed or canceled — the same safeguard voters in Perry, Ohio, had just voted to require.
items.source: Payaries (summarizing Axios, Fortune and CNBC reporting)

items.title: Giant pandas return to Atlanta after a two-year absence
items.summary:
Zoo Atlanta's panda habitat stood empty for two years. That ended Friday, November 6, when Ping Ping, a male, and Fu Shuang, a female, made their public debut in the newly renovated Arthur M. Blank Panda Grove, with crowds expected to line up for a first look.

The two 6-year-olds arrived from China in September under a 10-year loan agreement and spent weeks getting acclimated out of public view. Both were born at the Chengdu Research Base of Giant Panda Breeding — Ping Ping in March 2020 and Fu Shuang in October 2020 — and the new habitat, funded by a $6 million grant, adds expanded indoor spaces, climbing structures, pools and water features. Zoo members get early-morning viewing through November 22.

Atlanta's previous four pandas returned to China two years ago, ending a 25-year run at the zoo amid strained U.S.-China relations. The new agreement, between the zoo and the China Wildlife Conservation Association, restarts that partnership and makes Zoo Atlanta one of only three U.S. zoos housing giant pandas, and the only one in the Southeast — alongside San Diego and Washington's National Zoo.

Beyond the crowds, the debut is a small piece of diplomacy. China has long loaned pandas as a gesture of goodwill and let agreements lapse when tensions rise, so a fresh 10-year deal in Atlanta is read as a modestly warmer signal. For Atlanta families, the simpler meaning is the one the zoo is selling: a beloved exhibit is back, in a better home, for the next decade.

items.title: Browns will start Shedeur Sanders at Saints with Watson in concussion protocol
items.summary:
Cleveland will turn to Shedeur Sanders on Sunday in New Orleans, after head coach Todd Monken confirmed Friday that the second-year quarterback will make his first start of the season against the Saints. Deshaun Watson remains in the concussion protocol and is listed as questionable, with no decision yet on whether he could even serve as the backup if he is not cleared.

The change traces back to the loss at Pittsburgh, where Watson took a helmet-to-helmet hit early in the first quarter, was evaluated and returned, then reported symptoms on Tuesday morning and entered the protocol. Sanders took all of the first-team practice reps this week. He has thrown only three passes in spot duty this season, but he split first-team reps during the summer competition before Watson won the job in late August.

As a rookie in 2025, Sanders started the final seven games, throwing for 1,400 yards with seven touchdowns and ten interceptions and going 3-4. Monken pointed to improved footwork, mechanics, and speed through progressions and protections as signs of growth since then. Sanders himself said last year's starts showed him what he needed to work on, and that the offseason was spent on exactly those areas.

For a 5-3 Browns team trying to bounce back from a 27-6 loss, the stakes are immediate. A win in New Orleans keeps Cleveland in the AFC North race; a slow start has been a season-long problem, with the Browns averaging very little offense in first quarters. Dillon Gabriel, back from injured reserve, could back up Sanders, with rookie Taylen Green as the emergency option.

items.title: Cavaliers rout 76ers 119-95, hold LeBron James to 8 points in his Cleveland return
items.summary:
Cleveland got its revenge on Friday night, beating Philadelphia 119-95 in an NBA Cup game at Rocket Arena after the 76ers had come back from 29 points down to beat the Cavs in the season opener. Donovan Mitchell led Cleveland with 23 points, seven rebounds and eight assists, and Evan Mobley added 22, as the Cavs controlled the game from a 33-22 first quarter onward.

The headline inside the blowout was LeBron James' quiet return to Northeast Ohio. Now with Philadelphia after choosing the 76ers over a third stint in Cleveland in the offseason, James was held to eight points on 3-of-12 shooting with six turnovers in 31 minutes. It was only the tenth single-digit scoring game of his 24-year regular-season career, and it snapped a 396-game streak of scoring in double figures in Cleveland. Philadelphia's five-game winning streak ended, and the 76ers fell to 8-2 despite still leading the East.

Cleveland did it short-handed. Starting center Jarrett Allen was out with a right knee contusion suffered November 4 at Oklahoma City, and Sam Merrill left at halftime with a right elbow injury. Peyton Watson, back after missing two games with right hamstring tightness, changed the game defensively — 13 points, nine rebounds, and strong work on Tyrese Maxey and at the rim — while rookie Meleek Thomas scored 12, Mario Hezonja had 15 points and 10 rebounds, and Thomas Bryant added 13 in 15 minutes.

The win lifts Cleveland to 5-4 and gives the young rotation a confidence result, but there is no rest. The Cavs host the New York Knicks tonight at 8 p.m. on the second night of a back-to-back, with Allen's availability still unresolved and the Knicks arriving on two days' rest.

items.title: No. 12 Ohio State hosts No. 23 Oregon today in a playoff survival game — with backup quarterbacks on both sides
items.summary:
Ohio Stadium hosts one of the biggest games of the day on Saturday, with No. 12 Ohio State facing No. 23 Oregon at 3:30 p.m. ET on CBS. Ohio State is 6-2 after a 30-18 loss to USC last week; Oregon is 5-3. The Buckeyes are favored by 7.5 points, with a total around 46.5.

Neither team has its original starting quarterback. Oregon's Dante Moore is out for the season after a concussion against USC in September, leaving Dylan Raiola to lead the Ducks. Ohio State's Julian Sayin is out indefinitely, according to coach Ryan Day, leaving freshman Luke Fahey to deal with an Oregon pass rush led by Teitum Tuioti and Matayo Uiagalelei — a protection problem that hurt the Buckeyes a week ago.

The playoff math is unforgiving. Ohio State sat just outside the projected 12-team field in the first College Football Playoff rankings, listed as the first team out, while Oregon needs to win out to stay alive. A second loss already put Ohio State on the brink; a third would likely end its playoff hopes with Michigan still to come on November 14.

Expect a low-scoring, physical game at home. The Dispatch panel leaned Ohio State in a close one, and the market does the same, but Oregon's defensive front makes this a genuine test of whether the Buckeyes can protect a young quarterback well enough to keep their season alive.

items.title: Ohio State basketball finds its 'blueprint' in 89-65 home-opening win over Youngstown State
items.summary:
Ohio State got its first win of the season on Friday night, pulling away from Youngstown State 89-65 at the Schottenstein Center after the Penguins had cut the lead to 53-52 with just over ten minutes to play. It was a needed response after the Buckeyes opened the season with a loss to a ranked BYU team.

The turning point came inside, which was not the expected script for a perimeter-heavy team. Center Andrija Jelavic and forward Amare Bynum scored all 13 points in a 13-0 run that broke the game open, capped by a Bynum fast-break dunk off a Jelavic steal. Ohio State outscored Youngstown State 36-13 over the final 10:20. Jelavic finished with 21 points and nine rebounds, Bynum with 15 and eight, and guard John Mobley Jr. led all scorers with 25.

At halftime the Buckeyes led only 38-33 and had shot 1-for-10 from three. Transfer guard Jimmie Williams addressed the team about ball and player movement, and the second half looked different — better sharing, better defense, and easy points off deflections and turnovers. Coach Jake Diebler singled out quieter contributions from LJ Smith and Justin Pippen as part of the growth.

Jelavic called the closing stretch the blueprint: connected offense, using size and length on defense, and rewarding the bigs when they run and play hard. Ohio State, now 1-1, hosts Marshall on Monday, November 9 at 6 p.m. ET on Big Ten Network.

items.title: Amy Acton becomes Ohio's first woman elected governor, Sherrod Brown returns to the U.S. Senate
items.summary:
Ohio made history on Election Day, November 3. Democrat Amy Acton, the physician who led the Ohio Department of Health during the early COVID pandemic, defeated Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become the first woman elected governor of Ohio and the first Democrat to win the office since Ted Strickland. With 87 percent of precincts reporting, she led about 51 percent to 46 percent in unofficial results.

In the U.S. Senate race, Democrat Sherrod Brown defeated Republican Jon Husted, who had been appointed to fill the seat JD Vance vacated to become vice president. Brown, returning two years after losing his previous seat, led about 49 percent to 47 percent with 86 percent counted, in a call made by NBC, CNN and the Associated Press. Acton said Ohio had chosen unity and decency, and pledged to be a governor for all Ohioans; Ramaswamy congratulated her in concession.

The night extended beyond the top races in Northeast Ohio. In the 7th District, Democrat Brian Poindexter unseated Republican Rep. Max Miller, and Cuyahoga County voters passed the developmental disabilities levy (Issue 10, near 63 percent) and the health and human services levy (Issue 11, about 60 percent). More than 1.7 million Ohioans voted early, a record for a governor's year, with Cuyahoga County leading the state in early voters. Statewide Issue 3, putting the photo voter ID law into the state constitution, was also projected to pass.

Results remain unofficial until county boards certify them within 21 days. Acton takes office in January 2027, and the transition — along with how a Democratic governor and a still-divided legislature handle budgets, health policy and elections law — will be the story in Columbus through the winter.

Cleveland Magazine CLE Daily version also returned: https://www.clevelandmagazine.com/articles/amy-acton-voted-governor-sherrod-brown-wins-cle-daily/

items.title: Cleveland misses out on $7.8 million federal lead grant after HUD deems city too risky
items.summary:
Cleveland has lost a new $7.8 million federal grant to make homes lead-safe, after the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development rejected the city's application. According to Signal Cleveland's reporting, HUD did not question the need — Cleveland's older housing stock makes lead a persistent risk for children — but rated the city itself too risky to manage the money.

The decision came from a broader risk review of how Cleveland handles federal housing dollars, including reporting, meeting goals, and finishing work on time, not just its lead programs. City officials said lead work has actually sped up, with about 100 housing units completed in the past year compared with roughly 40 over the five years before that, and that they are exploring an appeal after a debriefing with HUD. A city council member called the denial terrible news.

The timing makes the gap harder. Cleveland still has three older HUD lead grants in progress, but all are winding down: a $9.7 million Glenville grant closing at the end of November, a $2 million healthy homes grant closing next June, and a $5.7 million citywide grant closing next July. Without the new award, no fresh federal lead money is lined up to replace them.

For families and landlords, the legal duty does not change. Rental homes built before 1978 still need Lead Safe Certification, and the city is still enforcing it. What changes is how much public help may be available to pay for repairs — help that already has a waitlist, and that is now likely to get harder to reach.

baby.tip: Day 6 tip — feeding rhythm check: by now Benji should be feeding 8–12 times in 24 hours and making at least 5–6 wet diapers and several stools a day — those counts are the simplest at-home sign he's getting enough. Keep a quick tally on the shared tracker today; if counts dip or he's too sleepy to feed, that's an 'ask his pediatrician' call, not a wait-and-see.
baby.fact: At six days old, Benji can already focus best on faces about 8–12 inches away — exactly the distance to your face when you hold him to feed. His vision is still blurry beyond that, and high-contrast patterns hold his attention longest, which is why newborns stare so intently at faces.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for Day 6: a tummy-time minute on a firm surface while he's awake and watched — even 30 seconds counts at this age — with Moose on official supervisor duty from across the room. Name note: in 2026 Benjamin has been a top-10 boys' name in the U.S. for over a decade, so Benji already has plenty of namesakes.
